You can only find a file if you remember what you named it.

Foresight is an experimental Mac app from Google, running on EmbeddingGemma 2 and Gemma 4.
The model searches text, images, audio and video by description, not keywords. You don't need the filename, the exact phrase, or any memory of where you saved it.

So you can ask questions about your own work files, with the processing running locally on your machine.
A supplier asks what you agreed about the packaging. You don't remember and everyone's waiting on the call. Ask Foresight, and it searches your connected files and returns the answer with the source you can check, while you're still on the line.

Same for product specs, client approvals, project notes and past decisions.
It's experimental and Mac only right now, so treat it as a preview rather than something to build a process on.
But the bigger prize is obvious. Most company knowledge sits in one person's head, and work stops until they reply. That's a bottleneck you can actually remove.

Claude can build you a CRM. It may not be able to use the one you've already got.

Your inventory system, your legacy CRM, the internal tool someone built in 2019. No API, no accessibility tree. Nothing for an agent to hook into, so it guesses.

Claude and OpenAI's computer-use models can read a screenshot. They just misjudge where to click often enough that you can't hand them real work.

Cua Perception fixes that specific gap. A dedicated detector that finds text and icons on screen and gives the agent real coordinates. The model decides what to do, Cua Driver does the clicking and typing.

So: your team uses a custom inventory system, and checking an order means opening the app, searching the order number, confirming stock. The app exposes nothing readable. Perception locates the search field and buttons from the screen itself, and the agent works through it.

It runs locally on your CPU, so those internal screens never leave the machine. Worth knowing that coordinate-based automation is sensitive to redesigns, so expect to retest after a UI change.

The value isn't dramatic. It's the ninety-second lookup that happens twenty times a day and pulls someone off real work each time.
Teaching AI to operate the software you already own beats buying another AI app to sit next to it.

This is the ultimate storytelling framework for boring businesses.

It’s called the Story Pyramid.

And this is the easiest way to get people addicted to your content, even if you talk about super boring topics.

Comment LAUNCH to join my 4 week live content growth program (and level up your short-form storytelling).

Step 1 is to pick the right topic in the first place.

You want to pick subjects where there’s broad awareness in your category, but still aligns with the biggest pain points your viewer faces.

Don’t talk about things that are super obscure or not important to the viewer…because the TAM for those ideas is just too small.

Step 2 is to find a novel angle on that topic.

Content only works in 2 scenarios.

Either your topic is new and you tell me about it, or it’s old, but you wrap it in a new frame.

The best new frames come from some state change or reveal.

For example, if you make content about tax accounting.

What new laws have passed in the last 6 months that enabled strategies that weren’t possible before.

Step 3 is Contrast Framing.

When you write your scripts or speak in your content, position the new reality against the old way of doing things.

This comparison frame will make your new take feel more interesting.

People’s brains think in comparative relationships…so A vs B always works.

Step 4 is called Desire Anchoring.

As you explain the story, connect this new reveal with the desired outcome the viewer wants.

If you remind them of their desired outcome, and frame how this new thing will get them there, it will make them eager to keep watching.

These 4 steps together are a recipe for making anything interesting, even if it starts with a super boring topic.

This is why your content can’t hold viewer’s attention.

It’s because of something called the Hourglass Effect.

If there’s one reason why my videos have super high retention, it’s because I found a way to solve for this.

Every viewer has about 25 seconds of attention capacity in their brain.

Think of it like an hourglass that starts draining the second your video starts.

Even if you have the greatest hook of all time, the average viewer is going to leave when that 25 seconds is up.

Unless…you rehook them.

A rehook is a specific type of sentence that enables you to flip the hourglass back over.

This buys you another 25 seconds of attention, which dramatically increases watch time.

Now this seems like a little thing, but a great rehook can actually be the most valuable line in the entire script.

And the tactical method for writing them is actually very simple.

First, you want to identify the main interesting thing your viewer is thinking about.

This is usually whatever you set up in the intro of the video.

Then, you want to frame the rehook.

This is a transition from the first interesting thing to a second one.

If you can make that transition smooth, you will reset the hourglass and hold their attention for way longer.

Now the technique for writing rehooks is one of the most valuable storytelling skills you can learn.
